growth_story.headline: The Gambia's income per person drifted down for a generation; since the 2017 democratic transition it has grown 2.8 percent a year to a record high.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2016, income per person in the Gambia shrank by 0.2 percent a year on average, and in 2016 it stood below its 1990 level. World Bank staff link those years to frequent droughts, economic mismanagement and weak governance during the dictatorship that followed the 1994 coup. Since the democratic transition in 2017, income per person has grown 2.8 percent a year, lifted first by aid-financed public investment and then by remittances, tourism and construction. The pandemic broke the run in 2020, when tourist arrivals collapsed and income per person fell 1.8 percent, but growth resumed in 2021. The last decade averaged 2.4 percent a year, against -0.5 in the decade before. In 2025 income per person reached the highest level in a series that starts in 1966.

threads.title: A generation of drift
threads.text: Between 1990 and 2016 income per person went nowhere and often fell. The World Bank ties this to droughts, mismanagement and weak governance under the dictatorship that followed the 1994 coup, and describes income per person as stagnant for three decades.

threads.title: Democratic transition and donor support
threads.text: The turn in 2017 coincides with the end of the dictatorship. Growth after the transition was first carried by public investment paid for from abroad, and the World Bank still credits stable macro management, public investment and aid for the run since then.

threads.text: Tourism and remittances from Gambians abroad support private spending and investment. That left the economy exposed when the pandemic cut tourist flows in 2020, and both are still expected to lift household incomes today.

threads.title: Farming at the mercy of weather
threads.text: Rain-fed farming makes growth swing from year to year, and the World Bank traces the ups and downs mainly to frequent droughts. Farm output is again under strain as fertilizer has become harder to get.

since_last_year.text: Growth stayed strong through 2025, and income per person rose 3.6 percent that year to a new high. Since then the war in the Middle East has weighed on the outlook and tightened fertilizer supply, and the IMF and World Bank both expect growth to slow in 2026.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe robust growth in the whole economy since 2017. Income per person grew more slowly, at 2.8 percent a year, because the population also grew fast. The World Bank also notes that this growth has brought only limited gains in jobs and poverty reduction.
